prompt: Many students now use artificial intelligence tools to complete their homework and written assignments. What problems does this cause, and what measures could be taken to solve them?
promptCn: 如今许多学生使用人工智能工具来完成家庭作业和书面作业。这会带来哪些问题？可以采取哪些措施来解决？
ideas: 问题一：学生跳过了思考和写作的过程，作业交上去了，能力却没有练出来；例如每篇读后感都让 AI 代写的初中生，到了闭卷限时考试连一段完整的论证都组织不起来
问题二：老师无法判断作业是否反映学生的真实水平，反馈和成绩都失真；自己认真写的学生分数反而可能比只输入一句指令的同学低，打击努力的人
措施一：全面禁止难以执行，应改变评估方式——更多课堂内写作，例如历史老师花五分钟和每个学生当面讨论他的作业，让写作过程看得见
措施二：制定明确的使用规则（例如可以用 AI 检查语法、推荐资料，但不能生成整篇答案），并教学生发现 AI 输出中的错误
立场：与其一禁了之，不如调整作业和评估方式，并教学生负责任地使用
outline: Intro: describe how common AI homework tools have become; preview - the main problems are lost learning and unreliable assessment, and schools should change how work is set and marked
Body 1: problem 1 - students skip the thinking process that homework is meant to train
Body 2: problem 2 - teachers cannot judge real ability; honest students may be disadvantaged
Body 3: solutions - more writing in class, short conversations about submitted work, clear rules on acceptable AI use
Conclusion: restate the problems and argue that adapting assessment works better than a ban
phrases: move from novelty to everyday habit
the very process that sth is designed to train
send a damaging message about sth
modelAnswer:
Within a few years, AI writing tools have moved from novelty to everyday habit for many pupils, who can now produce a polished essay in seconds. Although the technology is not harmful in itself, its misuse creates serious problems for learning and assessment, and schools need to change how they set and mark work.

The most serious problem is that students skip the very process that homework is designed to train. Planning an argument, choosing evidence and rewriting a clumsy paragraph are difficult, but this struggle is how writing skills develop. A fourteen-year-old who asks a chatbot to produce every book review may submit excellent work all term, yet discover in a timed exam that she cannot organise a single paragraph on her own.

A second problem concerns fairness. When homework can be generated by software, teachers can no longer tell whether a piece of work reflects a pupil's real ability, so their feedback and grades become unreliable. In a class where half the students hand in AI-generated essays, for example, a hard-working boy who writes his own may receive a lower mark than classmates who typed a single instruction, which sends a damaging message about effort.

Since a complete ban would be almost impossible to enforce, the solution lies in changing assessment. Teachers could set more writing in class, and a history teacher, for instance, could spend five minutes with each pupil discussing their homework; a student who cannot explain an essay is unlikely to have written it. Schools should also publish clear rules on acceptable use, allowing AI to check grammar or suggest sources but not to produce whole answers, and teach students to spot the errors these tools often make.

To sum up, AI tools threaten both genuine learning and fair assessment. Rather than attempting a ban, schools should make the writing process visible and teach pupils to use the technology responsibly.

prompt: Some people believe that self-driving cars will make roads safer and should be introduced as soon as possible. Others think that the risks of this technology are too great. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
promptCn: 有人认为自动驾驶汽车会让道路更安全，应当尽快推广。也有人认为这项技术的风险太大。讨论两种观点并给出你自己的看法。
ideas: 支持尽快推广：多数交通事故源于人为失误——疲劳、分心看手机、酒驾，而电脑不会走神；例如从清晨一直开到半夜的长途货车司机
支持尽快推广：不能开车的人（如视力差的老人）可以独立出行，看朋友、去医院都不必依赖亲属接送
主张谨慎：软件可能误判少见情况，如事故现场交警用手势指挥、乡间道路积雪；系统可能被黑客入侵；出事后责任归乘客、车企还是软件公司不清楚
主张谨慎：大量出租车和送货司机可能失业
立场：应该推广，但要循序渐进——先在高速公路专用车道、机场航站楼之间的接驳线路等可控环境使用，同时先立法明确事故责任
outline: Intro: paraphrase both views; position - self-driving cars should be introduced, but gradually rather than as soon as possible
Body 1: the case for rapid adoption - most accidents are caused by human error; independence for people who cannot drive
Body 2: the case for caution - software errors in unusual situations, hacking, unclear legal responsibility, job losses
Body 3: own view - step-by-step introduction in controlled settings, with clear laws on liability
Conclusion: restate the balanced position
phrases: have good reasons to be cautious
modelAnswer:
Cars that can drive themselves are already being tested on public roads in several countries. Some people argue that they should be introduced as quickly as possible because they will save lives, while others believe the dangers are too serious. In my view, self-driving vehicles should be adopted, but gradually rather than in a rush.

Supporters point out that most road accidents are caused by human error. Drivers become tired, check their phones or drink alcohol, whereas a computer never loses concentration. A lorry driver who has been at the wheel since dawn, for example, is far more likely to make a fatal mistake at midnight than an automated system. Self-driving cars could also transform the lives of people who cannot drive, such as elderly people with poor eyesight, allowing them to visit friends or attend medical appointments without relying on relatives.

On the other hand, critics have good reasons to be cautious. Software that performs well on a sunny motorway may misjudge an unusual situation, such as a police officer directing traffic by hand after an accident or a country road covered in snow. There are also fears that criminals could hack into vehicles, and it remains unclear who would be responsible after a crash: the passenger, the manufacturer or the software company. In addition, large numbers of taxi and delivery drivers could lose their jobs.

I believe the sensible approach is to introduce the technology step by step. Driverless vehicles could first operate in controlled environments where conditions are predictable, for instance on dedicated motorway lanes or on shuttle routes between airport terminals. Meanwhile, governments should pass clear laws on liability before automated cars become widespread.

Overall, self-driving cars have the potential to make roads much safer, but the risks are too significant to ignore. A gradual introduction, supported by firm regulation, is the wisest way forward.

prompt: Many apps and websites now collect large amounts of personal information about their users. What problems can this cause, and what measures could be taken to protect people's privacy?
promptCn: 现在许多应用程序和网站会收集大量用户个人信息。这会带来哪些问题？可以采取哪些措施来保护人们的隐私？
ideas: 问题一：数据泄露——公司系统被黑客攻破后，用户的姓名、地址和银行信息落入犯罪分子手中，被用来实施精准诈骗；例如网店泄露信息后，退休教师收到冒充银行的邮件，被骗走积蓄
问题二：被用来操纵行为——平台分析搜索和浏览记录推送定向广告，甚至专挑人最脆弱的时候推送，例如向深夜刷赌博视频的年轻人推送博彩优惠
原因：隐私条款冗长、满是法律术语，大多数用户不看就点同意，并不知道自己交出了什么
措施一：政府立法限制收集范围，要求用几句平实的话说明收集什么、为什么收集；对保护不力的公司处以足以改变其行为的重罚
措施二：个人关闭不必要的定位权限（如手电筒、计算器应用）；学校在中学第一年就教学生检查应用权限
outline: Intro: describe how much personal data apps collect; preview - this exposes people to fraud and manipulation, and both governments and individuals need to act
Body 1: problem 1 - stolen data is used by criminals for fraud
Body 2: problem 2 - data is used to influence behaviour; users rarely understand privacy policies
Body 3: solutions - strict limits on collection, plain-language explanations, heavy fines; individuals checking app permissions
Conclusion: summarise the problems and solutions
phrases: end up in the hands of criminals
in ways that sb never agreed to
fines large enough to change sb's behaviour
modelAnswer:
Every time people download an app or visit a website, they leave behind information about their location, interests and habits, and much of it is stored by companies. This large-scale collection of personal data can cause real harm, and protecting users requires action from both governments and individuals.

The most immediate danger is that stored data can be stolen. When a company's systems are hacked, the names, addresses and bank details of millions of customers may end up in the hands of criminals. A retired teacher whose details are leaked by an online shop, for instance, might later receive a convincing email that appears to come from her bank and lose her savings to fraud.

Personal data can also be used to influence behaviour in ways that users never agreed to. Platforms analyse what people search for and how long they look at certain posts, then show them targeted advertisements. A young man who often watches gambling videos late at night may be shown betting offers at exactly the moment he is most vulnerable. Most users are unaware of this because privacy policies are long and full of legal language, so they simply click to accept them.

To tackle these problems, governments should strictly limit the information companies may collect and require them to explain, in a few plain sentences, what they gather and why. Firms that fail to protect data should face fines large enough to change their behaviour. Individuals can also help, for example by switching off location tracking for apps that do not need it, such as torch or calculator apps. Schools could support this by teaching pupils in their first year of secondary school how to check app permissions.

In short, careless data collection exposes people to fraud and manipulation. Firm regulation, combined with more careful habits among users, would give people far greater control over their personal information.

prompt: In many countries, governments are encouraging people to replace petrol and diesel cars with electric vehicles. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
promptCn: 在许多国家，政府鼓励人们用电动汽车取代汽油车和柴油车。这一发展的利是否大于弊？
ideas: 优点：电动车行驶时没有尾气，城市空气更干净，沿繁忙主干道步行上学的孩子和哮喘患者受益最大
优点：电力来自风能、太阳能时，全生命周期碳排放远低于燃油车；晚上在家充电比加满一箱油便宜，使用成本低
缺点：购车价格高，低收入家庭负担不起；充电不便，例如住在没有私人车位的公寓里的护士，上完十二小时夜班还得去公共充电桩排队
缺点：电池需要开采锂、钴等金属，破坏地貌，部分国家的矿工工作条件危险
立场：利大于弊——政府可以在居民街道装充电桩（如把充电器装在路灯杆上），制定严格的电池回收标准，同时继续投资公交、铁路和自行车道
outline: Intro: paraphrase the policy; position - the benefits are greater, although electric cars are not a complete solution
Body 1: advantages - cleaner city air, lower lifetime emissions with renewable electricity, lower running costs
Body 2: disadvantages - high purchase prices, difficulty charging, environmental and human cost of mining battery metals
Body 3: how the drawbacks can be reduced - street charging points, battery recycling standards, continued investment in public transport
Conclusion: restate that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages
phrases: put sth out of reach for sb
modelAnswer:
Many governments now offer tax breaks and grants to persuade drivers to switch from petrol and diesel cars to electric models. Although this shift has some genuine drawbacks, I believe its advantages are more significant.

The clearest benefit is cleaner air in towns and cities. Electric cars produce no exhaust fumes, so children who walk to school along busy main roads would breathe in far fewer harmful particles, and people with asthma would suffer fewer attacks. When the electricity comes from wind or solar power, these vehicles also generate much lower carbon emissions over their lifetime than conventional cars. For drivers, running costs are lower too, since charging a car overnight at home is considerably cheaper than filling a tank with petrol.

Nevertheless, the disadvantages are real. Electric cars remain expensive to buy, which puts them out of reach for many low-income families. Charging is another obstacle: a nurse who lives in a flat without a private parking space may have to queue at a public charger after a twelve-hour night shift. Moreover, batteries require metals such as lithium and cobalt, and mining them can scar landscapes and expose workers in some countries to dangerous conditions.

However, most of these problems can be reduced. Governments can install charging points on residential streets, as some cities have done by fitting chargers to lamp posts so that residents without driveways can charge overnight, and set strict standards for recycling old batteries. It is also important to remember that electric cars are only part of the answer; investment in buses, trains and cycle lanes must continue so that fewer journeys require a car at all.

On balance, encouraging electric vehicles is a sensible policy. Provided that governments make electric cars easier to afford and charge, and reduce the environmental impact of batteries, the benefits of this development clearly outweigh its drawbacks.

prompt: Some people believe that every secondary school should employ a full-time counsellor to support students' mental health, even if this means spending less on other areas. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
promptCn: 有人认为，每所中学都应聘请一名全职心理咨询师来支持学生的心理健康，即使这意味着其他方面的开支要减少。你在多大程度上同意或不同意？
ideas: 支持理由一：考试压力、网络欺凌、家庭矛盾让青少年焦虑和抑郁越来越常见，小问题早干预能防止恶化；例如考前失眠的十六岁女生，几周辅导就能恢复，没人管则可能直接辍学
支持理由二：校内咨询师触手可及——校外心理门诊常要排几个月，有些孩子也不愿告诉父母；被欺凌的男生午休时就能直接去敲门，不需要转诊，也不需要大人开车接送
让步：学校经费有限，削减图书、实验室和体育设施的开支同样会伤害学生
回应：心理健康本身就是学习的前提，焦虑到无法集中注意力的学生，新课本也帮不了他；经费特别紧张时，两所乡村小学校可以共享一名隔天轮流到岗的咨询师，或由地方卫生部门分担费用
立场：基本同意
outline: Intro: rising concern about teenage mental health; position - largely agree
Body 1: reason 1 - mental health problems are increasingly common and are best treated early
Body 2: reason 2 - a counsellor in school is far easier to reach than outside services
Body 3: concession - tight budgets; response - mental health underpins learning, and costs can be shared
Conclusion: restate agreement
phrases: The main argument in favour is that ...
modelAnswer:
Concern about the mental health of teenagers has grown sharply in recent years. It has therefore been suggested that every secondary school should employ a full-time counsellor, even if other budgets must be reduced. I largely agree with this view.

The main argument in favour is that psychological problems among young people are increasingly common and are best treated early. Exam pressure, online bullying and difficulties at home can all leave students anxious or depressed, and minor problems that are ignored often become serious ones. A sixteen-year-old who stops sleeping before her final exams, for instance, may recover quickly with a few weeks of support, whereas the same student left alone might drop out of school entirely.

Furthermore, a counsellor based in school is far easier to reach than outside services. In many areas, young people must wait several months for an appointment at a mental health clinic, and some are reluctant to tell their parents that they need help. A boy who is being bullied could simply knock on the counsellor's door during his lunch break, without needing a referral or a lift from an adult.

Admittedly, school budgets are limited, and cutting spending on books, laboratories or sports facilities would also harm students. Nevertheless, mental health is not separate from education; a pupil who is too anxious to concentrate gains little from new textbooks. Where money is especially tight, two small village schools could share one counsellor who works at each on alternate days, or local health services could contribute to the cost.

All things considered, I believe the benefits of employing school counsellors justify the expense. Early, easily accessible support can stop many young people's difficulties from turning into crises, and this ultimately helps them to succeed in their studies.

prompt: Many people now search the internet for information about their symptoms before, or instead of, visiting a doctor. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?
promptCn: 如今许多人在看医生之前，甚至代替看医生，先上网搜索自己的症状。为什么会出现这种情况？这是积极的还是消极的发展？
ideas: 原因一：网上信息免费、即时，而很多国家看家庭医生要等几天甚至几周；例如周一早上起了皮疹的上班族，最早只能约到下周，又不方便请假
原因二：有人觉得为私密问题看医生很尴尬，或者怕浪费忙碌的医生的时间
积极面：国家卫生部门等权威网站会说明哪些症状可以在家处理、哪些需要急诊；例如幼儿半夜低烧，家长可以判断能否等到天亮；了解过病情的病人问诊时问题也更清楚
消极面：网上信息良莠不齐，外行难以判断——普通紧张性头痛的人深夜读到脑瘤而恐慌好几天；更危险的是把胸痛当成消化不良而延误救治
立场：作为看医生的补充是有益的，但用来代替看医生是消极的发展
outline: Intro: paraphrase; preview - the habit is driven by convenience; it is mainly negative when it replaces professional advice
Body 1: causes - free, instant information; long waits for appointments; embarrassment about minor problems
Body 2: positive side - reliable websites help people decide whether they need a doctor and ask better questions
Body 3: negative side - inaccurate information, needless panic, dangerous delays in treatment
Conclusion: summarise the causes; restate that it is harmful when used instead of a doctor
phrases: type sth into a search engine
modelAnswer:
When people feel unwell nowadays, their first step is often to type their symptoms into a search engine rather than contact a doctor. This habit has spread mainly because online information is quick and convenient, and although it has some benefits, I believe it is largely a negative development when it replaces professional advice.

The main reason for this trend is convenience. Information on the internet is free and available instantly, whereas in many countries patients must wait days or even weeks to see a family doctor. An office worker who develops a rash on a Monday morning, for instance, may find that the earliest appointment is next week and that she cannot easily take time off work. Some people also feel embarrassed about discussing personal problems, or worry about wasting a busy doctor's time.

Admittedly, searching online can be useful. Reliable health websites, such as those run by national health services, explain which symptoms can be treated at home and which require urgent attention. A parent whose toddler develops a mild fever at night, for example, can check whether it is safe to wait until morning. Patients who have read about their condition may also ask better questions during appointments.

However, much of the information online is inaccurate or misleading, and people without medical training struggle to interpret it. A man with an ordinary tension headache may read about brain tumours late at night and spend days in unnecessary panic. More dangerously, someone may decide that chest pain is simply indigestion and delay seeking help until it is too late. A doctor can examine a patient and arrange tests, which no website can do.

To summarise, people look up medical information online because it is fast, free and avoids the wait for an appointment. Although trustworthy websites can complement professional care, using the internet instead of a doctor is, in my view, a harmful trend.

prompt: Some people believe that employees who are able to do their jobs from home should be allowed to work from home whenever they wish. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
promptCn: 有人认为，能够在家完成工作的员工应该可以随时选择在家办公。你在多大程度上同意或不同意？
ideas: 同意的部分：省去通勤的时间和费用，例如每天在拥挤列车上花两小时的会计，可以用这段时间锻炼或接孩子放学
同意的部分：远离开放式办公室的噪音更专注；需要照顾年幼孩子或年迈亲属的员工更容易兼顾
反对完全自由：很多经验是在办公室里非正式学到的，比如旁听同事处理棘手电话、随口问邻座问题；刚毕业的新员工通过视频会议学到的远少于坐在资深同事旁边几个月
反对完全自由：长期独自在家容易孤独，晚上难以从工作中抽离
立场：部分同意——应慷慨地允许远程办公，但团队约定固定到岗日（如每周二、周四），而不是完全随心所欲
outline: Intro: the spread of home working; position - partly agree: remote work should be widely available, but not unlimited
Body 1: benefits of choice - no commute, better concentration, easier to balance work and family
Body 2: problems with unlimited freedom - less informal learning for new staff, isolation, difficulty switching off
Body 3: compromise - agreed office days for each team, home working for the rest of the week
Conclusion: restate partial agreement
phrases: find it hard to switch off
keep most of the benefits of sth
modelAnswer:
Since the pandemic, millions of office workers have discovered that much of their work can be done from a kitchen table. Some people now argue that these employees should be free to work at home whenever they like. While I agree that remote work should be widely available, I do not believe the choice should be completely unlimited.

There are strong reasons to give staff more freedom. Working from home removes the daily commute, which saves both time and money. An accountant who spends two hours a day on crowded trains could instead use that time to exercise or collect her children from school. Many people also concentrate better away from the noise of an open-plan office, and those caring for young children or elderly relatives find it easier to balance their responsibilities.

However, if every employee could stay at home whenever they wished, teamwork would suffer. Much useful knowledge is learned informally, by overhearing how a colleague handles a difficult phone call or by asking a quick question at the next desk. A graduate in his first job, for example, is likely to learn far less from video calls than from sitting beside experienced colleagues for several months. In addition, some people who work alone for weeks feel isolated and find it hard to switch off in the evening.

A sensible compromise is for each team to agree on fixed office days. A design team might meet in person on Tuesdays and Thursdays for planning and training, while members work from home for the rest of the week. This arrangement keeps most of the benefits of remote work while ensuring that new staff receive the guidance they need.

On the whole, working from home offers clear advantages, and employers should be generous in allowing it. However, a balance between home and office serves both workers and companies better than complete freedom of choice.

prompt: A growing number of people now work as freelancers or find short-term jobs through mobile apps, such as food delivery and taxi services, instead of having a permanent job with one employer. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
promptCn: 越来越多的人以自由职业者身份工作，或通过手机应用接短期工作（如外卖配送和网约车），而不是在一家单位做长期固定工作。这一趋势的利是否大于弊？
ideas: 优点：时间自由，适合有其他安排的人；例如大学生只在周五、周六晚上送餐，不耽误上课；家长只在孩子上学时接单
优点：门槛低，刚被裁员的人几天内就能开始挣钱，而不用等上几个月
缺点：收入不稳定，淡季订单骤减；大多没有病假工资、带薪假期和养老金缴费，例如冬天摔断手腕的司机六周没有收入，而正式员工照常领薪
缺点：派单和评分由算法控制，拒单或迟到就会被降分；大城市的外卖骑手为了多跑单每天工作十二小时、冒雨在车流里穿行，安全受到威胁
立场：对想赚点外快的人是好选择，但对以此为全职收入的人弊大于利，除非政府保障病假工资和最低收入等基本权利
outline: Intro: describe the rise of app-based and freelance work; position - the disadvantages are greater for those who depend on it as their main income
Body 1: advantages - flexibility for students and parents; quick access to income
Body 2: disadvantage 1 - unpredictable income; no sick pay, holiday pay or pension
Body 3: disadvantage 2 - control by algorithms; pressure to work long hours and take risks
Conclusion: restate that the drawbacks outweigh the benefits unless basic protections are introduced
phrases: The barriers to entry are low.
modelAnswer:
In many cities, a large part of the workforce no longer has a single employer. Instead, people deliver food, drive passengers or complete design projects for whoever pays them through an app. Although this kind of work offers genuine flexibility, I believe its disadvantages are greater, particularly for those who depend on it as their main source of income.

The chief attraction of these jobs is freedom. Workers can decide when and how much to work, which suits people with other commitments. A university student, for example, can deliver meals on Friday and Saturday evenings without missing lectures, and a parent can accept jobs only while the children are at school. The barriers to entry are also low, so someone who has just been made redundant can start earning within days rather than months.

However, this freedom comes at a high price. Income is unpredictable, since the number of orders can fall sharply during a quiet week, and most app-based workers receive no sick pay, holiday pay or pension contributions. A driver who breaks his wrist in winter may have no income at all for six weeks, whereas a permanent employee in the same situation would continue to be paid.

Equally worrying is the pressure these workers are under. Their tasks are allocated by algorithms, and their ratings can drop if they turn down orders or arrive late. As a result, a delivery rider in a large city may feel forced to work twelve-hour days and weave through heavy traffic in the rain to complete as many orders as possible, which puts his safety at serious risk.

Taking everything into account, freelance and app-based work is a useful option for people who want to earn some extra money. For the many who rely on it full-time, however, the insecurity and lack of protection outweigh the flexibility, unless governments guarantee basic rights such as sick pay and minimum earnings.

prompt: Some people believe that parents should be punished, for example by being fined, when their children commit crimes. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
promptCn: 有人认为，当孩子犯罪时，应该惩罚其父母，例如处以罚款。你在多大程度上同意或不同意？
ideas: 支持方理由：父母依法负有监护责任，罚款能促使疏于管教的父母重视起来；例如任由十三岁孩子每天凌晨两点还在外面、从不过问去了哪里的家庭
反驳一：多数少年犯的父母已经尽力，只是孩子被当地团伙拉走；例如在养老院上夜班的单亲妈妈无法每晚看着儿子，罚她等于惩罚她无法控制的处境
反驳二：罚款对低收入家庭打击最大，经济压力加剧家庭争吵，反而把孩子推得更远
替代方案：法院要求父母参加为期十二周的育儿课程，社工帮助家庭定规矩、为青少年找晚间足球俱乐部等活动；只对明显失职、拒绝参加课程的父母处罚
立场：大体不同意，只在明显失职时追究父母责任
outline: Intro: paraphrase; position - mostly disagree, except in cases of obvious neglect
Body 1: concede the argument - parents are responsible for supervision; penalties might push careless parents to act
Body 2: objections - many parents are already trying hard; fines hit poor families hardest and increase stress at home
Body 3: alternative - compulsory parenting courses and family support; penalties only for clear neglect
Conclusion: restate the position
phrases: be drawn into a local gang
modelAnswer:
When teenagers break the law, it is natural to ask where their parents were. Some people therefore believe that mothers and fathers should be fined, or punished in other ways, for their children's crimes. Although parents clearly have an important role, I mostly disagree with this idea, except in cases of obvious neglect.

Supporters argue that parents are legally responsible for supervising their children, and that a financial penalty would force careless parents to take this duty seriously. If a family allows a thirteen-year-old to stay out until two o'clock every morning without ever asking where he has been, it seems reasonable to hold the adults partly accountable when he is caught damaging cars.

However, in most cases punishing parents would be both unfair and counterproductive. Many young offenders come from homes where the parents are doing their best but have lost influence over a child who has been drawn into a local gang. A single mother working night shifts in a care home, for example, cannot watch her son every evening, and fining her would punish her for circumstances beyond her control. Moreover, fines fall most heavily on low-income families, and the extra financial strain could lead to more arguments at home, pushing the young person even further away.

A more effective approach would be to offer practical support. Courts could require the parents of young offenders to attend a twelve-week parenting course, while social workers help families set clear rules and find activities for teenagers, such as evening football clubs. Penalties should be reserved for parents who have clearly ignored their responsibilities, for instance by refusing to attend such programmes.

To conclude, while parents should certainly be involved when their children commit crimes, punishing them would usually do more harm than good. Support and guidance are far more likely to prevent young people from reoffending.

prompt: In many cities, large numbers of surveillance cameras have been installed in streets, stations and other public places. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
promptCn: 在许多城市，街道、车站和其他公共场所安装了大量监控摄像头。这一做法的利是否大于弊？
ideas: 优点：威慑作用，人们知道会被拍下就不敢偷窃、打架；案发后录像是重要证据，例如晚高峰地铁站台发生抢包，警方靠多个摄像头几小时内就能找到小偷
优点：让人更有安全感，尤其是深夜独自走路回家的女性；还能帮助寻找走失的儿童和患痴呆症的老人
缺点：普通人每天未经同意被拍几百次，信息可能被滥用；结合人脸识别后，当局可以追踪记者或和平示威者的行踪，压制言论自由
缺点：犯罪可能只是转移到没有摄像头的街道
立场：利大于弊，但需立法限制——规定录像保存期限（如三十天，调查需要除外）、只有受过培训的警员可以查看、由独立机构每年审查人脸识别的使用并公开结果
outline: Intro: paraphrase; position - the advantages are greater, provided that the use of footage is strictly controlled
Body 1: advantages - deterrence, evidence for investigations, a feeling of safety, finding missing people
Body 2: disadvantages - loss of privacy, misuse with facial recognition, crime moving elsewhere
Body 3: safeguards - limits on how long footage is kept and who may view it; independent oversight
Conclusion: restate that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages
phrases: arguments for regulation rather than for doing sth
modelAnswer:
Surveillance cameras have become a familiar sight on city streets, station platforms and in shopping centres. While this growth in monitoring raises legitimate concerns about privacy, I believe its benefits outweigh its drawbacks, provided that the use of the footage is strictly controlled.

The most important advantage is that cameras help to prevent and solve crime. People are less likely to steal or start fights when they know they are being filmed, and when offences do occur, recordings provide valuable evidence. If a commuter's bag is snatched on an underground platform during the evening rush hour, for example, footage from several cameras can allow police to trace the thief within hours. Cameras also make many people feel safer, especially women walking home alone late at night, and they have helped to find lost children and elderly people with dementia who have wandered away from home.

On the other hand, constant surveillance has serious disadvantages. Ordinary citizens may be recorded hundreds of times a day without their consent, and this information could be misused. When cameras are combined with facial recognition software, the authorities could track the movements of journalists or people attending a peaceful protest, which would discourage free expression. Furthermore, critics point out that cameras may simply move crime to streets where there are none.

These risks, however, are arguments for regulation rather than for removing cameras altogether. Laws should state how long recordings can be kept, perhaps thirty days unless they are needed for an investigation, and allow only trained police officers to view them. An independent body could also review the use of facial recognition every year and publish its findings.

All in all, surveillance cameras play a valuable role in keeping public places safe. As long as clear legal limits protect people's privacy, I am convinced that their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.

prompt: Some people think that newspapers and websites should not be allowed to publish stories about the private lives of famous people. Others believe that celebrities must accept this as part of being in the public eye. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
promptCn: 有人认为报纸和网站不应被允许刊登关于名人私生活的报道。也有人认为名人身处公众视野，必须接受这一点。讨论两种观点并给出你自己的看法。
ideas: 支持保护隐私：名人也有私生活的权利，狗仔跟拍造成巨大压力，还波及从未选择成名的家人；例如知名演员的孩子上学路上被摄影师尾随，无法过正常的童年
支持保护隐私：很多此类报道毫无公共价值，比如报道某位歌手胖了
另一方：很多名人主动寻求曝光、靠公众形象赚大钱，不能只在对自己有利时才接受关注
另一方：报道私生活有时能揭露虚伪和滥用权力，例如打着家庭价值观旗号竞选的政客被发现用公款与秘密情人度假，选民有权知道
立场：以公共利益为标准——足球明星偷税可以报道，同一球员和家人在海滩度假的照片不行；儿童在任何情况下都应受到保护
outline: Intro: paraphrase both views; position - celebrities deserve privacy unless a story genuinely serves the public interest
Body 1: arguments for privacy - harassment by photographers, harm to families, little real news value
Body 2: arguments for publishing - celebrities profit from publicity; exposing hypocrisy and abuse of power
Body 3: own view - a public interest test, with special protection for children
Conclusion: restate the position
modelAnswer:
Stories about the relationships, health and family problems of famous people sell newspapers and attract millions of clicks. Some argue that the media should be banned from publishing such stories, whereas others believe that intrusion is simply the price of fame. In my opinion, celebrities deserve privacy unless a story genuinely serves the public interest.

Those who favour stronger protection point out that famous people still have a right to a private life. Constant attention from photographers can cause severe stress, and the harm often extends to relatives who never chose to be in the public eye. The young children of a well-known actor, for example, may be followed by photographers on their way to school, which can leave them frightened and unable to lead a normal childhood. Moreover, many such stories have no real value; reporting that a singer has gained weight tells the public nothing important.

On the other hand, there are reasons why the private lives of public figures are sometimes reported. Many celebrities actively seek publicity and earn large sums from their public image, so they can hardly welcome attention only when it suits them. More importantly, revealing private behaviour can expose hypocrisy. If a politician who campaigns on family values is found to be using public money to pay for holidays with a secret partner, voters clearly have a right to know.

In my view, the key question is whether a story serves the public interest or merely satisfies curiosity. A report that a famous footballer is secretly avoiding tax would be justified, whereas photographs of the same player on a beach holiday with his family would not. Children, in particular, should be protected in all cases.

Ultimately, fame does not remove a person's right to privacy. Newspapers should remain free to expose wrongdoing and abuse of power, but they should not profit from intrusion that serves no wider purpose.

prompt: In many towns and regions, local newspapers are closing down because fewer people are willing to pay for them. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to solve them?
promptCn: 在许多城镇和地区，地方报纸因愿意付费阅读的人越来越少而纷纷停刊。这会带来哪些问题？可以采取什么措施来解决？
ideas: 问题一：没有记者旁听议会会议和法庭审理，地方政府在开支、规划上的决定无人监督；例如本地唯一一家报纸停刊几年后，议会把昂贵的建设合同交给某位议员的朋友也没人发现，浪费和腐败更容易发生
问题二：居民失去可靠的本地信息来源，转而依赖社区社交媒体群，谣言传得快；例如小学可能关闭的消息，家长一晚上就能读到十几条相互矛盾的帖子
问题三：共同的新闻来源消失，社区归属感减弱
措施一：非营利模式——读者会员费和慈善基金支持，例如几百位居民每月付一小笔钱，支撑一个专门报道地方政治的网络新闻编辑部
措施二：政府通过独立机构出资支付报道议会和法院的记者工资，但不干预报道内容；学校教学生识别可靠信息来源，提升对优质新闻的需求
outline: Intro: paraphrase; preview - closures weaken local democracy and community information, but there are practical solutions
Body 1: problem 1 - local councils and courts face less scrutiny
Body 2: problem 2 - residents rely on rumours in social media groups; a weaker sense of community
Body 3: solutions - non-profit membership models; independent public funding for local reporters; media education in schools
Conclusion: summarise the problems and solutions
phrases: make waste and corruption more likely
a reliable source of everyday information
a sense of belonging to sth
modelAnswer:
For generations, local newspapers reported on council meetings, court cases and community events. Today, as readers turn to free content online and advertising revenue moves to large technology companies, many of these papers are closing. This decline causes serious problems for local democracy, but there are practical ways to address it.

The most significant consequence is that local authorities face less scrutiny. When no reporter attends council meetings, decisions about spending, planning and public services can be made with little public attention. In a town whose only newspaper closed several years ago, for instance, a council could award an expensive building contract to a friend of a councillor without anyone outside the town hall noticing. Weak scrutiny of this kind makes waste and corruption more likely.

Residents also lose a reliable source of everyday information. Without trained journalists checking facts, people increasingly depend on neighbourhood social media groups, where rumours spread quickly. When a primary school announces that it may close, parents might read a dozen conflicting posts in a single evening, many of them inaccurate. Over time, the disappearance of shared news sources can also weaken people's sense of belonging to their community.

Several measures could help. Local news outlets could become non-profit organisations funded by reader memberships and charitable foundations; in some cities, a few hundred residents each pay a small monthly fee to support an online newsroom that covers local politics. Governments could also fund local reporting through an independent body that pays the salaries of journalists who cover councils and courts but has no control over what they write. In addition, schools could teach young people to recognise reliable sources, which would increase demand for quality journalism.

In summary, the loss of local newspapers reduces accountability and allows misinformation to spread. New funding models, independent public support and better media education could ensure that communities continue to receive trustworthy local news.

prompt: Some people believe that growing cities should build tall apartment blocks to house their populations. Others think that cities should expand outwards with low-rise houses. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
promptCn: 有人认为，不断扩大的城市应建造高层公寓楼来容纳人口。也有人认为城市应向外扩展，建造低层住宅。讨论两种观点并给出你自己的看法。
ideas: 建高楼的理由：节约土地，保护城市边缘的农田和森林；人口密度高，车站、商店在步行范围内，公共交通和本地服务才能维持，例如住在市中心高楼的年轻上班族完全不需要车
建低层的理由：带花园的住宅给孩子安全玩耍的空间，适合家庭生活；超高层容易让人孤立，电梯一坏，住在二十楼的老人就被困在家里
向外扩张的代价：新郊区要修路、铺管网、建学校，居民通勤距离长、依赖私家车，加剧拥堵和污染
立场：取中间方案——四到八层、围绕共享庭院和公园布置的中层住宅；例如巴黎市中心大多是六七层的建筑，却是欧洲人口最稠密的城市之一
outline: Intro: paraphrase both views; position - the best solution lies between the two extremes
Body 1: arguments for building upwards - efficient use of land, support for public transport and local services
Body 2: arguments for spreading outwards - gardens and family life, problems of very tall towers; but the costs of urban sprawl
Body 3: own view - medium-rise blocks around shared courtyards and parks
Conclusion: restate the position
phrases: have serious costs of its own
modelAnswer:
As urban populations grow, city planners must decide whether to build upwards or outwards. Some people favour tall apartment towers, while others prefer to extend cities with low-rise houses. In my view, the best solution lies somewhere between these two extremes.

Those who support high-rise housing argue that it uses land efficiently. By housing thousands of people on a small site, cities can protect the farmland and forests on their edges. Dense neighbourhoods also make public transport and local services viable: when enough residents live within walking distance of a station, frequent trains and a range of shops become profitable. A young professional living in a central tower block, for example, may be able to walk to the metro, the supermarket and the gym without ever needing a car.

Supporters of low-rise development, on the other hand, emphasise quality of life. Houses with gardens give children space to play safely and allow families to grow vegetables or simply enjoy fresh air. Very tall towers can feel isolating, and they create practical difficulties; an elderly woman living on the twentieth floor may be trapped in her flat whenever the lift breaks down. Nevertheless, spreading outwards has serious costs of its own. New suburbs require roads, pipes and schools, and residents often face long commutes by car, which increases congestion and pollution.

For these reasons, I believe cities should focus on medium-rise housing. Apartment buildings of around four to eight storeys, arranged around shared courtyards and parks, can house large numbers of people while keeping a human scale. Central Paris, for instance, consists largely of buildings of six or seven storeys, yet it is one of the most densely populated cities in Europe.

Weighing up both sides, neither towering skyscrapers nor endless suburbs offer an ideal answer. Medium-rise neighbourhoods with plenty of green space combine the efficiency of high-rise living with the comfort of more traditional housing.

prompt: In many countries, young people are leaving rural areas to live and work in cities. Why is this happening? What effects does this have on the communities they leave behind?
promptCn: 在许多国家，年轻人正离开农村地区到城市生活和工作。为什么会出现这种情况？这对他们离开的社区有什么影响？
ideas: 原因一：城市岗位多、工资高，而农业机械化让农村就业减少；学工程、设计的年轻人在小村庄找不到对口工作
原因二：大学集中在城市，十八岁离家读书的学生往往在城里建立起事业和朋友圈后就不再回来；城市娱乐和文化生活也更丰富
影响一：人口老龄化、萎缩，公共服务难以维持；例如只有十几名学生的村小被迫与二十公里外的学校合并，学校一关年轻家庭更不愿搬来，公交、商店和诊所也随之消失
影响二：独居老人缺人照顾，例如八十多岁的鳏夫可能好几天不跟任何人说话；传统手艺和地方节日后继无人
让步：外出者寄钱回家能改善家庭生活，但抵不上劳动人口的流失
outline: Intro: paraphrase; preview - work and education draw young people away, leaving villages older and more isolated
Body 1: causes - more and better-paid jobs, mechanised farming, universities and urban lifestyles
Body 2: effect 1 - an ageing, shrinking population and the closure of schools, buses and shops
Body 3: effect 2 - loneliness among older residents and lost traditions; money sent home only partly compensates
Conclusion: summarise the causes and effects
phrases: in search of a better life
Local services become difficult to sustain.
be forced to merge with sth
modelAnswer:
Across the world, villages are emptying as young people move to cities in search of a better life. This migration is driven mainly by economic and educational opportunities, and it is leaving many rural communities older, poorer and more isolated.

The most obvious reason is work. Cities offer a far wider range of jobs and usually pay higher wages, whereas employment in the countryside has declined as machines have replaced farm labourers. A young person with a degree in engineering or design is unlikely to find a suitable position in a small farming village. Education is another factor: universities are concentrated in urban areas, and many students who leave home at eighteen build their careers and friendships in the city and never return. The variety of entertainment and cultural life adds to the attraction.

The communities left behind suffer in several ways. As the population ages and shrinks, local services become difficult to sustain. A village primary school with only a dozen pupils may be forced to merge with one twenty kilometres away, and once the school closes, young families are even less likely to settle there. Bus routes, shops and doctors' surgeries often follow the same path, making daily life harder for those who remain.

There are social consequences too. Many elderly residents live alone with no relatives nearby, and a widower in his eighties might go several days without speaking to anyone. Traditional skills and local festivals may also disappear when there is no younger generation to continue them. Admittedly, some migrants send money home, which can raise their families' living standards, but this rarely compensates for the loss of an active working population.

In short, young people move to cities for jobs, education and a livelier lifestyle. Their departure leaves rural areas with ageing populations, declining services and increasingly isolated older residents.

prompt: Some people believe that every country should aim to produce all the food it needs rather than relying on imports from other countries. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
promptCn: 有人认为，每个国家都应力求自己生产所需的全部粮食，而不是依赖从其他国家进口。你在多大程度上同意或不同意？
ideas: 支持理由一：粮食安全——战争、疫情和突然的出口禁令可能切断供应；例如粮食出口大国限制小麦出口时，依赖进口面粉的国家几周内面包价格就会飞涨
支持理由二：扶持本国农民和农村就业，减少跨洋运输产生的排放
反对理由一：气候和地理条件差异巨大，沙漠国家自种小麦要抽取大量稀缺的地下水，寒冷的北方国家只能在加温温室里种热带水果；价格上涨、选择减少
反对理由二：贸易本身就是保障——遭遇旱灾的国家可以从丰收地区买粮，完全自给的国家反而无处求援
立场：部分同意——保持主粮的基本生产能力和应急储备（如够全国吃几个月的大米或小麦），其余继续依靠贸易
outline: Intro: paraphrase; position - partly agree: countries should protect their ability to grow staple foods, but complete self-sufficiency is unrealistic
Body 1: arguments for self-sufficiency - food security in a crisis, support for farmers, fewer shipping emissions
Body 2: arguments against - climate and geography, higher prices and less variety; trade as insurance against bad harvests
Body 3: balanced approach - basic production of staples and emergency reserves, with trade for everything else
Conclusion: restate partial agreement
modelAnswer:
Recent disruptions to global supply chains have led some people to argue that every nation should grow all of its own food. While I agree that countries should not depend too heavily on imports for basic staples, I believe that complete self-sufficiency is neither realistic nor desirable.

The strongest argument for producing food at home is security. Wars, pandemics and sudden export bans can cut off supplies with little warning. When a major grain-exporting country restricts its sales of wheat, for example, families in nations that import most of their flour may see the price of bread rise sharply within weeks. Growing more food domestically also supports farmers and rural jobs, and it reduces the emissions created by shipping products across oceans.

However, insisting that every country grow everything would be extremely costly. Climate and geography vary enormously: a desert state that tried to produce all its own wheat would need to pump vast amounts of scarce groundwater, while a cold northern country could only grow tropical fruit in heated greenhouses. Prices would rise, and consumers would lose much of the variety they currently enjoy. Ironically, trade also provides protection, since a country hit by drought can buy grain from regions where the harvest was good, whereas a fully self-sufficient nation would have nowhere to turn.

A more sensible approach is for governments to maintain a reasonable capacity to produce staple foods, together with emergency reserves of grain, while continuing to import other products. Some countries already store enough rice or wheat to feed their population for several months, which protects them from short-term shocks without sacrificing the benefits of trade.

All things considered, I only partly agree with this idea. Every country should be able to feed its citizens in an emergency, but complete self-sufficiency would raise prices, waste resources and, in many cases, make food supplies less secure rather than more.

prompt: English is increasingly used around the world in business, higher education and entertainment. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?
promptCn: 英语在世界各地的商业、高等教育和娱乐领域中使用得越来越广泛。为什么会出现这种情况？这是积极的还是消极的发展？
ideas: 原因一：英语国家（尤其是美国）经济和文化影响力大，跨国公司、国际组织和科学期刊默认使用英语；网上大量内容——从软件教程到热门影视剧——都是英文的
原因二：家长把流利的英语看作通往好工作的通行证；荷兰等国的大学用英语开设大量学位课程来吸引国际学生
积极面：不同国家的人可以直接沟通，省去翻译的成本和延误，例如巴西工程师和韩国客户一次视频会议就能解决技术问题；各国学生能第一时间读到最新研究
消极面：非母语者在申请国际职位和向期刊投稿时处于劣势；年轻人学习、工作、娱乐都用英语，本族语地位下降，有的社区青少年只在和祖父母说话时才用本地语言
立场：总体积极，前提是英语作为母语之外的补充，而不是替代
outline: Intro: paraphrase; preview - economic power and the internet explain the spread; it is positive overall if local languages are protected
Body 1: causes - the influence of English-speaking countries, multinational companies, research and online content; parents and universities
Body 2: positive effects - direct communication across borders; faster access to knowledge
Body 3: negative effects - disadvantages for non-native speakers; pressure on local and minority languages
Conclusion: restate that the trend is positive if English is learned in addition to, not instead of, mother tongues
phrases: come at the expense of sth
a passport to a good career
without the cost and delay of translation
in addition to sth, not instead of it
modelAnswer:
From boardrooms in Tokyo to lecture halls in Amsterdam, English has become the common language of much of the modern world. This spread can be explained by economic power and technology, and I believe it is a largely positive development, provided that it does not come at the expense of local languages.

Several factors explain the dominance of English. The economic and cultural influence of English-speaking countries, particularly the United States, has made English the default choice for multinational companies, international organisations and scientific journals. The internet has reinforced this trend, as a large share of online content, from software tutorials to popular films and series, is produced in English. Consequently, parents increasingly see fluency as a passport to a good career, and universities in countries such as the Netherlands now teach many degree courses in English to attract international students.

The benefits of a shared language are considerable. People from different countries can communicate directly, without the cost and delay of translation. A Brazilian engineer and a Korean client, for instance, can solve a technical problem together in a single video call. Students everywhere can also read the latest research as soon as it is published, rather than waiting years for a translation that may never appear.

Nevertheless, there are real drawbacks. Non-native speakers are often disadvantaged when applying for international jobs or submitting research to journals, even when their ideas are excellent. More worryingly, when young people use English for study, work and entertainment, their own languages may gradually lose status. In some communities, teenagers now speak the local language only with their grandparents, which threatens its survival.

On balance, the growth of English as a global language brings more benefits than problems. However, governments and schools should ensure that English is learned in addition to people's mother tongues, not instead of them.

prompt: Some governments are considering giving every adult citizen a fixed sum of money each month, whether or not they work. Do the advantages of this idea outweigh the disadvantages?
promptCn: 一些国家的政府正在考虑每月给每位成年公民发放一笔固定金额，无论其是否工作。这一设想的利是否大于弊？
ideas: 优点：人人领取同样金额，不需要复杂的表格和审核，没人会从福利体系的缝隙中漏掉；也消除了一找到工作就失去补助的福利陷阱
优点：给人们重新培训或照顾家人的自由；例如工作被自动化取代的工厂工人，可以花一年考护理资格而不陷入贫困
缺点：成本巨大，只能靠大幅加税或削减医院、学校等公共服务；钱也发给了不需要的人——高薪律师和失业青少年领一样多
缺点：部分人可能减少工作时间，护理、医院夜班等本就难招人的岗位更缺人；大城市房东可能因为租客多了收入而涨租，抵消补助的实际价值
立场：目前弊大于利，改进面向真正有需要人群的定向福利更现实
outline: Intro: explain the idea of a universal basic income; position - the disadvantages currently outweigh the advantages
Body 1: advantages - a simple safety net with no benefit trap; freedom to retrain or care for relatives
Body 2: disadvantage 1 - enormous cost; money paid to people who do not need it
Body 3: disadvantage 2 - fewer working hours in hard-to-fill jobs; higher rents
Conclusion: restate the position; targeted support is more practical
phrases: fall through the gaps in sth
an efficient use of limited funds
jobs that are already hard to fill
reduce the real value of sth
modelAnswer:
The idea of a universal basic income, a regular payment given to every adult regardless of their income or employment, has attracted growing attention in recent years. Supporters see it as a modern safety net, but I believe that its disadvantages currently outweigh its advantages.

The scheme certainly has attractive features. Because everyone would receive the same amount, there would be no complicated forms or assessments, and nobody would fall through the gaps in the welfare system. It would also remove a common trap in existing benefit systems, where people lose support as soon as they find paid work. Moreover, a guaranteed income could give people the freedom to retrain or care for relatives; a factory worker whose job has been automated, for example, could spend a year studying for a nursing qualification without falling into poverty.

The main problem, however, is cost. Paying even a modest monthly sum to every adult would require enormous public spending, which could only be funded through much higher taxes or cuts to services such as hospitals and schools. Much of this money would also go to people who do not need it. A lawyer earning a high salary would receive exactly the same payment as an unemployed teenager, which is hardly an efficient use of limited funds.

There are also concerns about the wider economy. Some people might choose to work fewer hours, which could worsen shortages in jobs that are already hard to fill, such as care work or night shifts in hospitals. In addition, landlords in expensive cities might raise rents once they knew that every tenant had extra income, reducing the real value of the payment.

To conclude, a universal basic income is an appealing idea, but its high cost and uncertain economic effects make it a risky policy. Improving targeted support for those in genuine need would be a more practical way to reduce poverty.

prompt: Some people believe that those who move to live in another country should adopt the customs and way of life of their new home. Others think they should keep their own traditions. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
promptCn: 有人认为，移居他国的人应该接受新国家的习俗和生活方式。也有人认为他们应该保留自己的传统。讨论两种观点并给出你自己的看法。
ideas: 主张融入：学习当地语言和日常社交规则，求职、交友和办事都更容易；例如不会当地语言的新移民母亲，看病时说不清孩子的症状，家长会上也无法和老师沟通
主张融入：如果新移民群体与当地人完全各过各的，社区之间的误解和不信任会加深
主张保留：饮食、节日、宗教和语言是身份认同和归属感的来源，放弃它们会让人觉得哪里都不属于；孩子也需要知道父母来自哪里
主张保留：接收国也因多元文化而更丰富，例如许多英国城镇在圣诞节之外也庆祝排灯节和春节，各种背景的居民都参与
立场：两者并不冲突——在工作、学校等公共生活中遵守法律、学习语言和习俗，在家庭和社区中保留母语、饮食和节日（如在德国的土耳其家庭在家说土耳其语）
outline: Intro: paraphrase both views; position - migrants can and should do both
Body 1: arguments for adopting local customs - language and social norms help with work and services; separate lives breed mistrust
Body 2: arguments for keeping traditions - identity, children's roots, enrichment of the host society
Body 3: own view - adapt in public life, keep traditions at home and in the community
Conclusion: restate that integration does not require giving up one's heritage
modelAnswer:
Millions of people now live outside the country where they were born, and there is considerable debate about how they should approach the culture of their new home. Some believe that newcomers ought to adopt local customs, while others argue that they should preserve their own. In my view, migrants can and should do both.

Those who emphasise adaptation make a valid point. Learning the local language and understanding everyday social rules make it much easier for migrants to find work, make friends and deal with public services. A newly arrived mother who cannot speak the language, for instance, may struggle to explain her child's symptoms to a doctor or discuss her son's progress at a parents' evening. On a wider scale, if groups of newcomers live entirely separate lives, misunderstanding and mistrust between communities can grow.

On the other hand, traditions are an important source of identity. Food, festivals, religion and language connect people to their families and their past, and abandoning them can leave migrants feeling that they belong nowhere. Children, in particular, benefit from knowing where their parents come from. Furthermore, host societies are often enriched by the cultures that migrants bring; many British towns, for example, now celebrate Diwali and Chinese New Year as well as Christmas, with events that attract residents of every background.

I believe these positions are not really in conflict. Migrants should respect the laws of their new country and make a genuine effort to learn its language and customs in public life, such as at work and at school. At the same time, there is no reason why a Turkish family in Germany should not speak Turkish at home, cook traditional dishes and celebrate their own festivals.

Taking everything into account, integration does not require people to give up who they are. The most successful approach combines participation in the wider society with pride in one's own heritage.

prompt: In many countries, fewer young people are choosing to study science subjects at university. What are the reasons for this, and what can be done to encourage more students to study science?
promptCn: 在许多国家，选择在大学攻读理科专业的年轻人越来越少。原因是什么？可以采取什么措施鼓励更多学生学习理科？
ideas: 原因一：中学理科常被教成背公式应付考试，缺少实验；招不到专业教师的学校由其他学科的老师代上物理课，只能照本宣科；抄了两年公式的十五岁学生不太可能选物理专业
原因二：理科学位实验课时长、数学难，回报却不确定；例如在化学和商科之间犹豫的十七岁学生，会觉得商科毕业生付出少得多却挣得更多；学生也不了解科学家每天实际做什么
原因三：刻板印象——女生仍会被告知工程和物理是男生的学科
措施一：让课堂更实用，例如用一个学期检测本地河流的水质并向镇议会汇报结果；提高薪资吸引专业理科教师
措施二：大学和企业提供奖学金和实习机会，邀请在职科学家（尤其是女性）走进中学
outline: Intro: paraphrase; preview - the decline stems from how science is taught and perceived, and it can be reversed
Body 1: cause 1 - science taught as memorisation; shortage of specialist teachers
Body 2: cause 2 - demanding degrees with uncertain rewards; little knowledge of scientific careers; stereotypes
Body 3: solutions - practical project-based lessons, better pay for specialist teachers, scholarships, internships and visiting scientists
Conclusion: summarise the causes and solutions
phrases: a list of formulas to memorise
modelAnswer:
Scientific knowledge drives progress in medicine, energy and technology, yet in many countries the number of students choosing science degrees is falling. This decline stems largely from the way science is taught and perceived at school, and it can be reversed through better teaching and closer links with scientific careers.

One major cause lies in secondary education. Many teenagers experience science as a list of formulas to memorise for exams rather than a way of investigating the world. In schools that cannot recruit specialist teachers, physics may be taught by someone trained in another subject, who understandably relies on the textbook rather than experiments. A fifteen-year-old who has spent two years copying equations from the board is unlikely to choose physics at university.

Students are also put off by the nature of science degrees and the careers that follow. These courses involve long hours in laboratories and difficult mathematics, yet the rewards seem uncertain. A seventeen-year-old choosing between chemistry and business, for instance, may conclude that business graduates earn more for considerably less effort. Many young people have no idea what scientists actually do, beyond the image of a researcher in a white coat. Stereotypes play a part too: girls are still sometimes told that engineering and physics are subjects for boys.

To address these problems, schools should make lessons more practical. Students might, for example, spend a term testing the water quality of a local river and present their findings to the town council, which shows that science can solve real problems. Governments could offer higher salaries to attract specialist teachers, while universities and companies could provide scholarships and internships and invite working scientists, especially women, into schools.

To sum up, science is losing students because it is often taught in a dull way and its careers are poorly understood. Engaging lessons, well-qualified teachers and visible role models could inspire a new generation to study it.

prompt: In some countries, many people no longer trust the advice of scientists and other experts. Why might this be the case? What can be done to increase public trust in science?
promptCn: 在一些国家，许多人不再信任科学家和其他专家的建议。为什么会出现这种情况？可以采取什么措施增强公众对科学的信任？
ideas: 原因一：公众误解科学的运作方式——科学会随新证据修正结论，却被看成专家前后矛盾；例如九十年代被告知鸡蛋伤心脏、后来又读到鸡蛋完全健康的购物者，会怀疑一切饮食建议
原因二：社交媒体放大了问题，关于副作用的戏剧性个人故事能传给几百万人，严谨的统计证据却很少传得那么快
原因三：资金问题——新药研究由卖这种药的公司出钱，病人和医生自然怀疑结果是否客观；偶发的数据造假丑闻加深了这种印象
措施一：科学家用平实的语言解释研究，坦诚说明不确定性（建议基于现有证据、可能随研究改变）；研究机构公开每项研究的资助方
措施二：学校教授科学方法本身——让十六岁的学生了解同行评审如何运作、练习判断网络信息来源的可靠性
outline: Intro: paraphrase; preview - distrust stems from misunderstandings about how science works, misinformation and concerns about funding; openness and education can rebuild it
Body 1: causes - changing advice seen as inconsistency; misinformation on social media
Body 2: cause - research paid for by interested companies; occasional scandals
Body 3: solutions - plain, honest communication about uncertainty; transparency about funding; teaching the scientific method
Conclusion: summarise the causes and solutions
phrases: be better equipped to do sth
modelAnswer:
In recent years, warnings from doctors, climate researchers and other specialists have often been met with suspicion rather than respect. This loss of trust has several causes, including misunderstandings about how science works, the spread of misinformation and concerns about money, but it can be addressed through greater openness and better education.

One reason is that the public often misinterprets the way scientific knowledge develops. Science advances by revising its conclusions when new evidence appears, yet many people see such changes as a sign that experts do not know what they are talking about. A shopper who was told in the 1990s that eggs were bad for the heart, and later read that they are perfectly healthy, may reasonably wonder why any dietary advice should be believed. Social media makes the problem worse, as a dramatic personal story about a side effect can reach millions of people, while careful statistical evidence rarely spreads as quickly.

Concerns about funding also damage trust. When research on a new medicine is paid for by the company that sells it, patients and doctors naturally question whether the results are objective. Occasional scandals, in which researchers have been caught inventing data, reinforce the impression that scientists cannot always be trusted.

Several steps could help to rebuild confidence. Scientists should explain their findings in plain language and be honest about uncertainty, making clear, for instance, that a recommendation is based on current evidence and may change as studies continue. Research institutions should also publish who funds each study. Most importantly, schools could teach the scientific method itself; if sixteen-year-olds learn how peer review works and practise judging the reliability of online sources, they will be better equipped to evaluate expert advice as adults.

Overall, public distrust of science arises from changing advice, misinformation and suspicion about funding. Clear communication, transparency and education in scientific thinking offer the best way to restore that trust.
